data.name: Home.Faq1.Q
data.value: Do I need to know music theory?

data.name: Home.Faq1.A
data.value: No. Every exercise comes with instructions and tips, and you can start with single notes before moving on to intervals and chords.

data.name: Home.Faq2.Q
data.value: Does it work on my phone?

data.name: Home.Faq2.A
data.value: Yes. It runs in the browser on phones, tablets and computers, with nothing to install. Headphones help. The singing exercises use the microphone, and your recording never leaves your device.

data.name: Home.Faq3.A
data.value: Portuguese (Brazil), English and French. You can switch at any time from the menu at the top of the page.

data.name: Home.Faq4.Q
data.value: I'm a teacher. How do I create a class?

data.name: Home.Faq4.A
data.value: Create your account and ask the administrator to enable the teacher profile. The teacher area then appears in the top menu, where you create classes, invite students by email and assign routines.

data.name: Home.Faq5.A
data.value: {0}, grouped by area: ear training, melody, harmony, scales and rhythm. They range from telling whether a second note is higher or lower to melodic and rhythmic dictation and singing into the microphone. The full list is above.

data.name: Home.Faq6.A
data.value: Yes. Creating an account and training cost nothing.

data.name: Exercise.GuessNote.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the note that plays and pick the matching note from the available options.

data.name: Exercise.GuessNote.Tip1
data.value: Listen more than once if you need to.

data.name: Exercise.GuessNote.Tip2
data.value: Try singing the note to compare with your inner reference.

data.name: Exercise.GuessNote.Tip3
data.value: Compare it to notes you know well, such as C or A.

data.name: Exercise.GuessChords.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the chord and select the matching chord type.

data.name: Exercise.GuessChords.Tip1
data.value: Pay attention to the feeling: major sounds happy, minor sounds sad.

data.name: Exercise.GuessChords.Tip2
data.value: Compare against reference chords if you need to.

data.name: Exercise.GuessChords.Tip3
data.value: Try singing the notes to feel whether the intervals are major or minor.

data.name: Exercise.GuessInterval.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the two notes and identify the distance between them (interval).

data.name: Exercise.GuessInterval.Tip1
data.value: Associate intervals with songs you know (e.g. major third = "Happy Birthday").

data.name: Exercise.GuessInterval.Tip2
data.value: Listen again and sing the notes.

data.name: Exercise.GuessInterval.Tip3
data.value: Notice whether the sound is close (second) or wide (fifth, octave...).

data.name: Exercise.GuessQuality.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the chord and name its quality: major, minor, diminished, augmented, a seventh chord, or a sus, 6 or add9 chord. The Chord type filter picks which ones are played.

data.name: Exercise.GuessQuality.Tip1
data.value: Try to memorize the typical sound of each quality.

data.name: Exercise.GuessQuality.Tip2
data.value: Diminished chords sound tense or unstable.

data.name: Exercise.GuessQuality.Tip3
data.value: Compare with simple chords you already know.

data.name: Exercise.GuessQuality.Tip4
data.value: A dominant 7 asks to resolve; a major 7 rests, soft and bright.

data.name: Exercise.GuessQuality.Tip5
data.value: Sus chords have no third: neither major nor minor, they sound open, waiting.

data.name: Exercise.GuessFunction.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the cadence that sets the key, then to the chord, and identify its function in that key (tonic, subdominant, dominant...).

data.name: Exercise.GuessFunction.Tip1
data.value: Listen to the whole progression first to anchor the key.

data.name: Exercise.GuessFunction.Tip2
data.value: The tonic feels like home; the dominant pulls back to it.

data.name: Exercise.GuessFunction.Tip3
data.value: Subdominant chords feel like a soft step away from the tonic.

data.name: Exercise.GuessDegree.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the cadence that sets the key, then to a note, and identify its degree in that key (1 is the tonic). In a minor key, the degrees are those of the natural minor scale: 3, 6 and 7 are a minor third, sixth and seventh above the tonic.

data.name: Exercise.GuessDegree.Tip1
data.value: Sing the scale up from the tonic until you reach the note.

data.name: Exercise.GuessDegree.Tip2
data.value: The leading tone (7 in a major key) pulls up to the tonic, and 4 leans down to 3.

data.name: Exercise.GuessDegree.Tip3
data.value: 1, 3 and 5 sound stable: they are the notes of the tonic chord.

data.name: Exercise.GuessFullInterval.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the interval and identify both the distance and its quality (major, minor, perfect, etc.).

data.name: Exercise.GuessFullInterval.Tip1
data.value: Identify the size first, then refine to the quality.

data.name: Exercise.GuessFullInterval.Tip2
data.value: Major and minor differ by one semitone.

data.name: Exercise.GuessMissingNote.Instructions
data.value: Listen to two melodies and tell whether they are the same or whether something changed.

data.name: Exercise.GuessMissingNote.Tip1
data.value: Pay attention to the central notes of the melody.

data.name: Exercise.GuessMissingNote.Tip2
data.value: If you are unsure, listen more than once.

data.name: Exercise.GuessMissingNote.Tip3
data.value: Singing or tapping the melody helps memorization.

data.name: Exercise.IntervalMelodico.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the melody and identify the first scale degree, the last one, and the intervals between the first two and the last two notes.

data.name: Exercise.IntervalMelodico.Tip1
data.value: Find the key of the melody first.

data.name: Exercise.IntervalMelodico.Tip2
data.value: Pay attention to the first and last notes to determine the degrees.

data.name: Exercise.IntervalMelodico.Tip3
data.value: Compare the intervals to ones you already know.

data.name: Exercise.IntervalMelodico.Tip4
data.value: Use scales as a reference for the degrees.

data.name: Exercise.SolfegeMelody.Instructions
data.value: Click “New melody” and read the melody on the staff. Listen to the starting note, click “Record” and sing the melody, then click “Validate”. Any octave is fine.

data.name: Exercise.SolfegeMelody.Tip1
data.value: Look carefully at the pitches on the staff.

data.name: Exercise.SolfegeMelody.Tip2
data.value: Sing slowly to make sure you are accurate.

data.name: Exercise.SolfegeMelody.Tip3
data.value: If needed, practice the scale before attempting.

data.name: Exercise.SolfegeMelody.Tip4
data.value: Your recording is analyzed in your browser and never leaves your device.

data.name: Exercise.HigherOrLower.Subtitle
data.value: Listen to two notes and decide whether the second note moved up or down.

data.name: Exercise.HigherOrLower.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the two notes in sequence, then choose whether the second note is higher or lower than the first.

data.name: Exercise.HigherOrLower.Tip1
data.value: Focus on the direction of the sound instead of trying to name each note.

data.name: Exercise.HigherOrLower.Tip2
data.value: Sing the first note, then notice whether your voice needs to move up or down.

data.name: Exercise.HigherOrLower.Tip3
data.value: Use a wider note range when you are ready for larger jumps.

data.name: Exercise.GuessScaleType.Subtitle
data.value: Identify whether a played scale is major, minor or pentatonic.

data.name: Exercise.GuessScaleType.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the complete scale and choose the scale type that matches its sound.

data.name: Exercise.GuessScaleType.Tip1
data.value: Major scales tend to sound bright and stable.

data.name: Exercise.GuessScaleType.Tip2
data.value: Minor scales tend to sound darker or more tense.

data.name: Exercise.GuessScaleType.Tip3
data.value: Pentatonic scales have fewer notes and a more open contour.

data.name: Exercise.GuessGreekMode.Subtitle
data.value: Recognize the seven Greek modes by ear.

data.name: Exercise.GuessGreekMode.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the modal scale and select the Greek mode being played.

data.name: Exercise.GuessGreekMode.Tip1
data.value: Ionian is the familiar major sound; Aeolian is the familiar natural minor sound.

data.name: Exercise.GuessGreekMode.Tip2
data.value: Dorian has a minor color with a raised sixth; Phrygian has a lowered second.

data.name: Exercise.GuessGreekMode.Tip3
data.value: Lydian feels bright because of its raised fourth; Locrian feels unstable because of its diminished fifth.

data.name: Exercise.GuessCadence.Subtitle
data.value: Hear a four-chord progression and identify the cadence.

data.name: Exercise.GuessCadence.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the progression. The first chords establish the key and the final motion defines the cadence.

data.name: Exercise.GuessCadence.Tip1
data.value: Perfect cadences sound resolved and final.

data.name: Exercise.GuessCadence.Tip2
data.value: Plagal cadences have the familiar “amen” IV to I sound.

data.name: Exercise.GuessCadence.Tip3
data.value: Imperfect cadences stop on V; deceptive cadences avoid the expected resolution.

data.name: Exercise.GuessInversion.Subtitle
data.value: Identify whether a triad is in root position, first inversion or second inversion.

data.name: Exercise.GuessInversion.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the chord and choose the inversion by focusing on the bass note and chord spacing.

data.name: Exercise.GuessInversion.Tip1
data.value: Root position has the chord root in the bass.

data.name: Exercise.GuessInversion.Tip2
data.value: First inversion places the third in the bass and often sounds lighter.

data.name: Exercise.GuessInversion.Tip3
data.value: Second inversion places the fifth in the bass and often sounds less settled.

data.name: Exercise.CompleteScale.Subtitle
data.value: Hear the tonic and complete the rest of the scale on the staff.

data.name: Exercise.CompleteScale.Instructions
data.value: Click Play to hear the tonic. Then use the staff editor to enter the remaining notes of the scale in ascending order.

data.name: Exercise.CompleteScale.Tip1
data.value: Major scale pattern: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.

data.name: Exercise.CompleteScale.Tip2
data.value: Natural minor pattern: whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole.

data.name: Exercise.CompleteScale.Tip3
data.value: Use sharps or flats after placing a note if the scale requires an accidental.

data.name: Exercise.CompleteChordText
data.value: Listen to the chord and write it on the staff.

data.name: Exercise.SelectStaffExerciseText
data.value: Generate the exercise and enter your answer on the staff before validating.

data.name: Exercise.CompleteChord.Prompt
data.value: Listen to the chord and complete it above {{0}}.

data.name: Exercise.CompleteChord.Subtitle
data.value: Hear a chord and write its notes on the staff.

data.name: Exercise.CompleteChord.Instructions
data.value: Click Play to hear the chord. Write its notes stacked on the staff, from the root up. If the root is already on the staff (in gray), write only the others.

data.name: Exercise.CompleteChord.Tip1
data.value: Major chords have a major third and a perfect fifth; minor chords, a minor third and a perfect fifth.

data.name: Exercise.CompleteChord.Tip2
data.value: A diminished chord has a diminished fifth, a half step below the perfect one; an augmented chord, an augmented fifth, a half step above.

data.name: Exercise.CompleteChord.Tip3
data.value: In seventh chords, listen for the seventh: major (a half step below the octave), minor (a whole step below) or diminished (a step and a half below).

data.name: Exercise.CompleteChord.PromptWhole
data.value: Listen to the chord and write all of its notes on the staff, with the root in octave {{0}}.

data.name: Exercise.TransposeScaleText
data.value: Listen to the original scale and write it in the target key.

data.name: Exercise.TransposeScale.Subtitle
data.value: Write a played scale transposed to a new key.

data.name: Exercise.TransposeScale.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the original scale, note the target key, and enter the transposed scale on the staff.

data.name: Exercise.TransposeScale.Tip1
data.value: Keep the same interval pattern in the new key.

data.name: Exercise.TransposeScale.Tip2
data.value: Start on the target tonic and move degree by degree.

data.name: Exercise.TransposeScale.Tip3
data.value: Use accidentals to preserve the scale pattern.

data.name: Exercise.MelodicDictationText
data.value: Listen to the melody and write the notes and rhythm.

data.name: Exercise.MelodicDictation.Subtitle
data.value: Hear a short melody and notate it on the staff.

data.name: Exercise.MelodicDictation.Instructions
data.value: A count-in gives the tempo, then the melody plays. Pick a note value, then click the note names in order; a rest takes one click. Barlines are added for you.

data.name: Exercise.MelodicDictation.Tip1
data.value: Listen once for the contour before entering notes.

data.name: Exercise.MelodicDictation.Tip2
data.value: Place the main durations first, then refine pitches.

data.name: Exercise.MelodicDictation.Tip3
data.value: Click a note on the staff to change its octave or accidental.

data.name: Exercise.RhythmDictationText
data.value: Listen to the rhythm and write the sequence.

data.name: Exercise.RhythmDictation.Subtitle
data.value: Hear a rhythm on one pitch and write the durations.

data.name: Exercise.RhythmDictation.Instructions
data.value: A count-in gives the tempo, then the rhythm plays. Click the note and rest values in the order you hear them. Barlines are added for you.

data.name: Exercise.RhythmDictation.Tip2
data.value: Identify long values before shorter ones.

data.name: Exercise.RhythmDictation.Tip3
data.value: A value that no longer fits in the measure is grayed out.

data.name: Exercise.GuessMeter.Subtitle
data.value: Hear the beats and tell how they group into bars.

data.name: Exercise.GuessMeter.Instructions
data.value: Listen to twelve beats and identify the meter. The first beat of each bar is accented: the beats group in twos (duple), threes (triple) or fours (quadruple).

data.name: Exercise.GuessMeter.Tip1
data.value: Count "1, 2, 3…" and go back to 1 on each accent: the highest number you reach is the meter.

data.name: Exercise.GuessMeter.Tip2
data.value: Duple and quadruple are easy to confuse: in quadruple, three weak beats separate the accents.

data.name: Exercise.GuessMeter.Tip3
data.value: With the accompaniment, the bass and the chord change mark the first beat, and the short chords the others.

data.name: Exercise.GuessRhythmPattern.Subtitle
data.value: Hear a rhythm and find it among four written ones.

data.name: Exercise.GuessRhythmPattern.Instructions
data.value: A count-in sets the tempo, then a two-bar rhythm plays. Pick, among the four written rhythms, the one you heard.

data.name: Exercise.GuessRhythmPattern.Tip1
data.value: The four rhythms differ in one or two beats: compare them before listening and look for where they change.

data.name: Exercise.GuessRhythmPattern.Tip2
data.value: Follow the score while you listen, counting the beats of each bar.

data.name: Exercise.GuessRhythmPattern.Tip3
data.value: The rhythms always differ in where their notes start: listen for the attacks more than for how long the notes last.

data.name: Exercise.RhythmPattern.Placeholder
data.value: Click Play to hear a rhythm and see the four choices.

data.name: Exercise.RhythmTap.Subtitle
data.value: Hear a rhythm and tap it back.

data.name: Exercise.RhythmTap.Instructions
data.value: A count-in sets the tempo, a two-bar rhythm plays, and the count-in plays again. On the next beat, tap the rhythm on the pad or with the space bar: one tap where each note starts.

data.name: Exercise.RhythmTap.Tip1
data.value: Count the beats while you listen, and keep counting through the second count-in: it sets the tempo of your taps.

data.name: Exercise.RhythmTap.Tip2
data.value: Only the attacks count: through long notes and rests, wait and count without tapping.

data.name: Exercise.RhythmTap.Tip3
data.value: You may start whenever you like after the count-in, and tap a little faster or slower: what counts is the time between your taps.

data.name: Exercise.RhythmTap.Placeholder
data.value: Click Play to hear a rhythm.

data.name: Exercise.RhythmTap.Listen
data.value: Listen, and wait for the second count-in to end…

data.name: Exercise.RhythmTap.Now
data.value: Now tap the rhythm, on the pad or with the space bar.

data.name: Exercise.GuessTopNoteText
data.value: Listen to the chord and identify the note on top.

data.name: Exercise.SelectGuessTopNoteText
data.value: Please select the note on top.

data.name: Exercise.GuessTopNote.Subtitle
data.value: Tell whether the root, the third or the fifth of a chord is on top.

data.name: Exercise.GuessTopNote.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the chord and identify which of its notes is on top, in the highest voice: the root, the third or the fifth. The bass is always the root.

data.name: Exercise.GuessTopNote.Tip1
data.value: Sing the highest note of the chord, as if it were the melody, then go down to the bass.

data.name: Exercise.GuessTopNote.Tip2
data.value: If the top note is the bass note in another octave, it is the root: the chord sounds settled.

data.name: Exercise.GuessTopNote.Tip3
data.value: The third on top sounds sweet and full; the fifth on top sounds open, as if the chord were left hanging.

data.name: Exercise.GuessInterval.Tip4
data.value: In a harmonic interval, sing the lower note, then the upper one: it becomes a melodic interval.

data.name: Exercise.GuessFullInterval.Tip4
data.value: Played together, seconds and sevenths sound harsh, thirds and sixths sound sweet, and fourths, fifths and octaves sound hollow.

data.name: Exercise.GuessChangedNoteText
data.value: Which note changed, and did it go up or down?

data.name: Exercise.SelectGuessChangedNoteText
data.value: Please select the note that changed and whether it went up or down.

data.name: Exercise.GuessChangedNote.Subtitle
data.value: Listen to two melodies and say which note changed and whether it went up or down.

data.name: Exercise.GuessChangedNote.Instructions
data.value: Listen to a melody, then to the same melody with one note changed. Say which note changed, counting from the first, and whether it went up or down.

data.name: Exercise.GuessChangedNote.Tip1
data.value: Count the notes as you listen: only one of them changes.

data.name: Exercise.GuessChangedNote.Tip2
data.value: Listen to each melody on its own with the Melody 1 and Melody 2 buttons.

data.name: Exercise.GuessChangedNote.Tip3
data.value: The note that changed moved one step along the scale or leapt a third; the others stay the same.

data.name: Exercise.GuessChangedNote.Tip4
data.value: The melodies end on the tonic: if the last note changed, the second melody doesn't sound finished.

data.name: Exercise.SingNote.Subtitle
data.value: Listen to a note and sing it.

data.name: Exercise.SingNote.Instructions
data.value: Click Play to hear a note. Click “Record”, sing the note on a vowel such as “ah”, then click “Validate”. Any octave is fine.

data.name: Exercise.SingNote.Tip1
data.value: Hum the note quietly before you record, then hold it steady for a second or two.

data.name: Exercise.SingNote.Tip2
data.value: When you get it right, the result says how close to the pitch you were, in cents: a hundred cents make a semitone.

data.name: Exercise.SingNote.Tip3
data.value: If a note is too high or too low for your voice, sing it an octave down or up, or narrow the octaves in the filters.

data.name: Exercise.SingNote.Tip4
data.value: Your recording is analyzed in your browser and never leaves your device.

data.name: Exercise.SingInterval.Subtitle
data.value: Sing the note you hear, then the interval from it.

data.name: Exercise.SingInterval.Instructions
data.value: Click Play to hear a note and see an interval. Click “Record”, sing the note, then the note that interval above or below it, and click “Validate”. Any octave is fine.

data.name: Exercise.SingInterval.Tip1
data.value: Sing the scale from the note in your head and stop on the interval’s degree: a 5th is the fifth note.

data.name: Exercise.SingInterval.Tip2
data.value: Take a short breath between the two notes, and hold each one for a second.

data.name: Exercise.SingInterval.Tip3
data.value: The Level filter chooses the intervals, and the Direction filter whether they go up or down.

data.name: Exercise.SingInterval.Tip4
data.value: Your recording is analyzed in your browser and never leaves your device.

data.value: Sing the note you hear, then this interval

data.name: Exercise.SingIntervalLevel.Medium

data.name: Exercise.SingIntervalLevel.All

data.name: Exercise.SingMelody.Subtitle
data.value: Listen to a short melody and sing it back.

data.name: Exercise.SingMelody.Instructions
data.value: Click Play to hear a short melody. Click “Record”, sing the melody, then click “Validate”. Any octave is fine.

data.name: Exercise.SingMelody.Tip1
data.value: Listen as many times as you need before you record: the melody moves by steps and thirds and ends on the tonic.

data.name: Exercise.SingMelody.Tip2
data.value: Sing each note on its own syllable, such as “la”, so the notes don’t blur together.

data.name: Exercise.SingMelody.Tip3
data.value: From four notes on, one wrong, missing or extra note is forgiven.

data.name: Exercise.SingMelody.Tip4
data.value: Your recording is analyzed in your browser and never leaves your device.

data.name: Exercise.GuessTuning.Subtitle
data.value: Hear a note twice and tell whether the second one is in tune, sharp or flat.

data.name: Exercise.GuessTuning.Instructions
data.value: Listen to the reference note, then to the same note played again. Tell whether the second one is in tune, sharp (too high) or flat (too low) compared with the first.

data.name: Exercise.GuessTuning.Tip1
data.value: Sing the first note and keep it in your head while the second one plays.

data.name: Exercise.GuessTuning.Tip2
data.value: Don't listen for a new note: listen for whether the second one leans up or down, like a string that needs tuning.

data.name: Exercise.GuessTuning.Tip3
data.value: Start at 50 cents (a quarter tone) and move to a smaller difference only once you get almost every round right.
